tags.description:
A customer approves a proof in the designer, and your storefront keeps it in
the cart until checkout. A proof does not wait forever: this guide is about
what to keep in the cart, when to commit the design, and what to do when a
cart outlives its proof.

## What a cart holds

`approve()` in the designer (or `POST /v1/proofs`) renders a proof and answers
a `proofToken` and a `proofUrl`. Keep the `proofToken` with the cart line, and
show the `proofUrl` to the customer as the picture of what they bought.

The token reaches you through the customer's browser, so treat the browser's
copy as untrusted: a customer can swap in another live proof of yours, of a
dearer template or product, and committing a token commits whatever proof it
names. Keep
the token with the cart line on your server once the line is priced, and
commit that copy rather than one the browser sends at checkout.

A proof can be committed for 7 days after it is rendered. Its `proofUrl` lives as long.

Nothing is stored as a design yet. A proof that is never committed costs you
nothing, and is cleaned up when it expires.

## Commit at checkout

Commit the design at checkout, before you take payment, from your server with
the secret key (a connected store, with its integration key), sending the
`proofToken` and any order details your printshop needs:

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs request -->
```json
{
  "proofToken": "eyJhdWQiOiJwcm9vZiIsImlkIjoicHJmXzljMWUyZDNmNGE1YjZjN2Q4ZTlmMGExYiIsInQiOiJhY21lIiwiZXhwIjoxNzkyNDkxMjQ3MDAwfQ.EXAMPLE_signature_not_a_real_one_0000000000",
  "fulfilmentPayload": { "variantSku": "TEE-BLACK-M" }
}
```

A committed design does not expire. It can still be corrected until it is
ordered, each correction a new revision, and a revision never changes once
made. Committing at
checkout rather than when the line is added means a cart the customer
abandons leaves no design behind.

## Check the design before you charge

The proof is made in the customer's browser, so a tampered page can make one
at a print size, template version, blank or placement the product does not
sell, and put it in a cheaper line. Once the design is committed, and before
you take payment for the line, read it with `GET /v1/designs/{id}` (the
secret or the integration key reads it) and check each of these against what
the line was priced as:

- `printSize`: the `widthMm` and `heightMm` the proof was made at.
- `templateBaseId` and `templateVersion`: the template and its version.
- `blankId` and `placementId`: the product and where on it the design
  prints.

When any of them differs, refuse the line and delete the design
(`DELETE /v1/designs/{id}`) rather than approve it.

To refuse such a line as soon as it is added rather than at checkout, commit
the design when the line is added instead, check it then, and keep the
design's id with the line in place of its `proofToken`. A cart the customer
abandons then leaves its design behind: delete it when the cart is dropped.

## Order details known only at checkout

A commit is refused with `422 missing_fulfilment_keys` when its
`fulfilmentPayload` lacks a key the printshop it goes to requires, and
`missing` names the keys. A design committed when the line is added cannot
carry what is known only once there is an order, such as Printful's
`recipient`: no one has said yet where it ships. A commit is not refused for
those keys. Send the ones you know at commit; the order is refused with
`missing_fulfilment_keys` when any required key is still missing when it is
placed. A commit with no `fulfilmentPayload` is checked as one with an empty
object.

A connected store's integration key hears no such refusal: its customer has
paid, so the order is answered `201`, written `failed` with `failureKind`
`missing_fulfilment_keys`, or `blank_needed` for a design on no blank at a
printshop that needs one, and the merchant is told. A member sends it to a
blank, or changes the default printshop, and submits it again.

The order itself can carry where it ships. Printful's `recipient` is not needed
in the payload for an order that sends its own `recipient` and
`shippingAddress`, or ships to a saved address: Printful ships to the order's.

## When the cart outlives the proof

Committing a proof past its expiry is refused, and nothing is committed:

- `410 proof_expired` — the token's time ran out, whether or not the proof
  has been cleaned up since.
- `404 unknown_proof` — the token is not a live proof of yours: it is not one
  Pixonaut signed for your account, or its proof is gone.

Either way the customer approves again: open the designer on the same
template with what they entered, and replace the cart line's `proofToken`
with the new one. To avoid asking at checkout, keep cart lines no longer
than a proof lives, or check a line's age when the customer returns to the
cart and ask them to approve it again then.
tags.name: Cart lifetimes and proof expiry

tags.description:
When a customer asks you to erase their personal data, what Pixonaut holds
for them depends on how far their purchase got. Each call below states, in
its own description, exactly what it removes and what it keeps.

## Before the design is ordered

A delivery given for a design's first order (`PUT /v1/designs/{id}/delivery`,
or the customer's answer on the address capture page) is held with the
design. Erase it with `DELETE /v1/designs/{id}/delivery`, using the secret
key or a connected store's integration key. It answers `204` whether there was a delivery or not, so it is safe to
call for every design the customer made.

## After the design is ordered

Once the design has an order, the order holds the recipient and the shipping
address, and the design's delivery no longer applies. Erase them with
`POST /v1/orders/{id}/erase-personal-data`, once the order has shipped,
failed or been cancelled. Until then it is refused `409 order_in_flight`, since the printshop
may still need the address. The order stays, its `recipient` and
`shippingAddress` now `null`, and `personalDataErasedAt` says when its data
was erased.

Find a customer's orders by your own reference with
`GET /v1/orders?externalRef=`. The reference is yours, and is not erased.

## What the customer put into a design

A design holds what its customer made: the text they typed, such as a name on
a shirt, and the pictures they uploaded, in each of its revisions, proofs and
prints. Erase them with `POST /v1/designs/{id}/erase-personal-data`, using
the secret key or the store's integration key, whatever the design's status:
approved and printed designs included. Call it for every design the customer
made.

- Every field the customer could fill is emptied, and every picture they
  uploaded is removed, in every revision. Text and pictures the template
  itself holds stay, so the design still says what was made from which
  template.
- Their request for changes and the delivery they gave are erased with them.
- The design stays: its template, status, dates and prints. It answers with
  `personalDataErasedAt` set, and `design.personal_data_erased` is sent to
  your webhook.
- The pictures and proofs are deleted within six hours.
- A print's files are kept while an order of it is still being made, since
  the printshop needs them, and deleted within six hours once every order of
  it has shipped, failed or been cancelled. An order whose outcome is unknown
  is not done, and keeps them until it is settled.
- Nothing more is printed, ordered, corrected, duplicated or asked to change
  from the design, and it takes no delivery: those calls answer
  `409 design_erased`.

Calling it again answers the design unchanged. A design you already deleted
is erased too, and answered `204`.

<!-- example: webhook design.personal_data_erased -->
```json
{
  "id": "1792022400000-8c2f4e1a-6b3d-4f7e-9a5c-1d0e8f7a6b52",
  "type": "design.personal_data_erased",
  "createdAt": 1792022400000,
  "payload": { "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c" }
}
```

## What is not erased

- The fulfilment payload is yours, written by your store, and stays with the
  design and its prints. Keep personal data out of it.
- A design duplicated from another is a design of its own: erase it too.
- No erasure reaches what a printshop was already sent.
tags.name: Erasing personal data

tags.description:
A shirt printed on the front and the back is one item: one order at the
printshop, one parcel, one charge. Each side is a design of its own,
committed for its own placement on the same blank, and printed on its own.
`POST /v1/orders` then orders the prints together, as one item.

## 1. Commit a design for each placement

Commit one design per side, each naming the blank and its own placement:

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs request -->
```json
{
  "templateId": "tshirt-back@1",
  "values": { "name": { "content": "Alexandra" } },
  "blankId": "blank_tshirt",
  "placementId": "back"
}
```

Approve each design and print it, as for any design
([Design to order](#tag/design-to-order)). You now hold a completed print of
each side.

### On the hosted designer, one link for both sides

A store that sends its customer to the hosted designer hands out one link for
the whole item: each side its own template, blank and placement, and the
size menu, photos and preselection it sells that side with. The page shows a
step per side, offers approving once the customer has opened every side, and
sends them back with a proof of each, under the side's `key`:

<!-- example: POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links request -->
```json
{
  "sides": [
    {
      "key": "front",
      "label": "Front",
      "templateId": "tshirt-front",
      "blankId": "blank_tshirt",
      "placementId": "front",
      "printSizes": [
        { "widthMm": 280, "heightMm": 360, "label": "Large" },
        { "widthMm": 200, "heightMm": 257, "label": "Medium" }
      ],
      "selectedPrintSizeIndex": 1
    },
    {
      "key": "back",
      "label": "Back",
      "templateId": "tshirt-back",
      "blankId": "blank_tshirt",
      "placementId": "back"
    }
  ],
  "returnUrl": "https://shop.example/cart",
  "state": "cart-10482",
  "locale": "sv"
}
```

The customer comes back to
`https://shop.example/cart?state=cart-10482&proofToken[front]=…&proofToken[back]=…`
(the brackets percent-encoded, which PHP reads as the array
`$_GET['proofToken']`), only once every side's proof is made. Commit each
side's proof with `POST /v1/designs` and its `proofToken`, then continue as
above. A link with `sides` must name a `returnUrl`, holds two to ten sides,
and names a side's options only in its entry. A side without `templateId` is
the path's template.

A designer is built for up to four sides: a garment's front, back and two
sleeves. A link with more is still made, and its response carries a warning
for you, never shown to the customer:

<!-- example: POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links 201 -->
```json
{
  "id": "shl_9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f",
  "token": "EXAMPLE_designer_link_token_not_a_real_one",
  "url": "https://app.pixonaut.example/h/design/EXAMPLE_designer_link_token_not_a_real_one?lang=sv",
  "expiresAt": 1791972000000,
  "name": null,
  "brandId": null,
  "designLimit": null,
  "printAreaFrame": false,
  "placementFrame": false,
  "locale": "sv",
  "warnings": [{ "code": "sides_over_recommended", "recommended": 4, "sides": 5 }]
}
```

Each side is one more step on the hosted page, one more designer, canvas and
photo set in the customer's browser, and one more `proofToken[<key>]` on the
return address. The SDK warns the same way, in the console, when it is mounted
with more than four `placements`.

## 2. Order the prints as one item

Send every print of the item, the one you think of as first first. The first
is the order's lead: the order's `printId` names it.

<!-- example: POST /v1/orders request -->
```json
{
  "prints": [
    { "printId": "c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f" },
    { "printId": "d5e6f7a8-b9c0-4d1e-8f2a-3b4c5d6e7f80" }
  ],
  "quantity": 1,
  "externalRef": "WEB-10482-1",
  "recipient": { "name": "Alexandra Lind", "email": "alexandra.lind@example.com" },
  "shippingAddress": {
    "company": "Lind Design AB",
    "line1": "12 High Street",
    "postalCode": "SW1A 1AA",
    "city": "London",
    "country": "GB"
  }
}
```

The order answers with every print, the lead first, and each print's
placement:

<!-- example: POST /v1/orders 201 -->
```json
{
  "id": "e1f2a3b4-c5d6-4e7f-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b",
  "tenantId": "acme",
  "printId": "c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f",
  "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
  "printIds": [
    "c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f",
    "d5e6f7a8-b9c0-4d1e-8f2a-3b4c5d6e7f80"
  ],
  "prints": [
    {
      "printId": "c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f",
      "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
      "designRevision": 1,
      "placementId": "front",
      "printedAs": "Front",
      "spotOutput": "process",
      "status": "completed",
      "placementFields": []
    },
    {
      "printId": "d5e6f7a8-b9c0-4d1e-8f2a-3b4c5d6e7f80",
      "designId": "7a2d9b3c-4e5f-4a6b-9c7d-8e9f0a1b2c3d",
      "designRevision": 1,
      "placementId": "back",
      "printedAs": "Back",
      "spotOutput": "process",
      "status": "completed",
      "placementFields": []
    }
  ],
  "adapter": "printful",
  "quantity": 1,
  "externalRef": "WEB-10482-1",
  "recipient": {
    "name": "Alexandra Lind",
    "email": "alexandra.lind@example.com"
  },
  "shippingAddress": {
    "company": "Lind Design AB",
    "line1": "12 High Street",
    "postalCode": "SW1A 1AA",
    "city": "London",
    "country": "GB"
  },
  "shipTo": null,
  "printshopConnectionId": "0b1c2d3e-4f5a-4b6c-8d7e-9f0a1b2c3d4e",
  "printshopName": "Printful",
  "spotOutput": "process",
  "externalOrderRef": "PF-889123",
  "status": "queued",
  "lastError": null,
  "failureKind": null,
  "hold": null,
  "tracking": null,
  "submittedAt": 1791886447000,
  "lastCheckedAt": null,
  "updatedAt": 1791886448000,
  "replacesOrderId": null,
  "replacedByOrderId": null,
  "personalDataErasedAt": null,
  "blankId": "blank_classic_tee",
  "variantRef": "v_3f9a1c2b7d4e8a01",
  "variant": {
    "ref": "v_3f9a1c2b7d4e8a01",
    "options": {
      "Color": "White",
      "Size": "M"
    },
    "fields": [
      {
        "name": "catalogVariantId",
        "value": "4012",
        "source": "own"
      }
    ]
  },
  "printshopAsPlaced": {
    "name": "Printful",
    "adapter": "printful"
  },
  "delivery": null,
  "blank": {
    "name": "Classic tee",
    "optionAxes": [
      "Color",
      "Size"
    ],
    "variants": 12
  }
}
```

Nothing is ordered, and the order is not written, when the prints are not one
item: a print committed before its placement was recorded
(`print_without_placement`), prints on different blanks, or some on a blank
and some on none (`mixed_blanks`), or two in one placement
(`duplicate_placement`). The same holds when the printshop cannot make them as
one item (`printshop_cannot_combine`), or when the designs disagree on what it
makes one item from, such as Printful's variant (`prints_disagree`, naming the
key). Each is a `422`.

### An item with no blank

A sign or a coaster printed on both faces has no blank: commit each face's
design with no `blankId` or `placementId`, and order the prints together as
above. Prints that are all on no blank are one item, with no placement to
compare. The order goes to the printshop the first print's design was
committed with, else the request's `printshopId`, else the workspace default;
with none it is refused `409 print_needs_printshop`. A print whose design was
committed with another printshop is refused `422 print_committed_elsewhere`,
naming it.

`order.submitted` and every later `order.*` event carry `printIds`. Find the
order by any of its prints with `GET /v1/orders?printId=`.

## 3. Hand each print's file to the printshop

A partner printshop receives every print as a file of the one item. A
printshop you describe yourself sends every print too, once its steps are
written to (its setup page in the docs says how). When you fetch the files
yourself, name the print:
`GET /v1/orders/{id}/job/files?printId=` and `GET /v1/orders/{id}/job/file?printId=`.
Without `printId` an order of several prints answers `422 print_id_required`,
naming its `printIds`.

## Cancelling before it is made

If the customer cancels before the item is made, `POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel`
asks the printshop to stop the whole item, and the order becomes `cancelled`
once it has. A printshop that has begun it answers `409 order_at_printshop`.
Refunding the customer stays yours.
tags.name: Front and back on one item

tags.description:
Your integration ships to stores that update it when they get round to it, so
it has to keep working while the API moves on. This guide is about what the API
promises between releases, and what you have to handle to hold it to that.

## Releases

The reference is released as a version, `info.version` in the document. Each
release is published with the reference it describes and a changelog of what
changed since the previous one. Pin a release, not whatever the API serves
today, and read the changelog before you move to the next.

A release is published in two places. The tag `api-v<version>` has a GitHub
release carrying `openapi.json`, `webhook-signature-vectors.json` and
`CHANGELOG.md`; that repository is private. Pixonaut's CDN serves the same
three files without a token, at

- `https://cdn.pixonaut.app/api/<version>/openapi.json`
- `https://cdn.pixonaut.app/api/<version>/webhook-signature-vectors.json`
- `https://cdn.pixonaut.app/api/<version>/CHANGELOG.md`

and `integrity.json` beside them lists each file's checksum. A published
version never changes, so an integration's CI pins a version and the checksum
of the file it fetched, and fails if either stops matching.

Versions follow what the reference did:

- a new major version may break a client written against the previous one;
- a new minor version only adds: an operation, an optional field, a value;
- a new patch version changes nothing you can rely on.

A breaking change made within a major version is listed in the changelog with
the reason it was agreed with the integrations it affects.

## Values that grow

A status, a refusal's `error` code and every other value the API sends from a
fixed set of possibilities is listed in the reference as an open set
(`x-extensible-enum`): the values known at this release. A later minor release
can add one. Handle a value you do not know instead of failing on it: treat an
unknown order status as still in progress, and an unknown refusal code by its
HTTP status, which keeps its meaning. A refusal names its code in `error`. The
fields beside it are optional in the reference, since a code added later may
not send them, and each one's description says which codes always do.

## Deprecated fields

A request field the API stops reading is deprecated before it is removed.
It is still accepted for 6 months from the day it is deprecated. While a field is deprecated, a request
that still sends it is answered as if it had not, and the response carries two
headers:

- `Deprecation`: when the field was deprecated, as `@` and Unix seconds;
- `Sunset`: the date it stops being accepted, as an HTTP date.

Log both when you see them: they are the notice to stop sending the field.
From the sunset on, a request sending it is refused `400` with
`field_removed`, naming the field in `field`. The reference marks a deprecated
field `deprecated`, with both dates.

A field whose absence would change what is made, counted or charged is not
ignored: dropping it quietly would turn your request into a different one. Such
a field is refused by name from the day it stops being read, with a code that
says where it went. How many copies to print moved to the order that way, so
`POST /v1/prints` refuses a `quantity` with `quantity_moved_to_order`.

## Deprecated response and webhook fields

A field the API stops sending, in a response or in a webhook's payload, is
deprecated before it goes, for the same window. Until its sunset it is still
sent; a field that was renamed is sent under its old name too, with the new
one's value. A response carrying one has the `Deprecation` and `Sunset`
headers; a webhook delivery does not, so read the reference's mark and the
release's changelog. From the sunset on the field is no longer sent. Move to
what the field's description says to read instead before then.

## Deprecated operations

An operation due to go is deprecated before it is removed, for the same
window. Until its sunset it answers as before, and every response carries the
`Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers. From the sunset on it is refused `410` with
`operation_removed`, naming it in `operation`. The reference marks the
operation `deprecated`, with its sunset in `x-sunset` and both dates in its
description.
tags.name: Versioning and deprecation

tags.description:
A storefront sends the same request more than once. A payment hook fires
twice, a job is retried after a timeout, a worker restarts halfway through.
Without care, each arrival commits a second design, renders a second print or
places a second physical order. This guide shows how to make every write in
the path safe to send again, how to tie Pixonaut's records to your own, and
how to clean up after a cart that was never bought.

## Send an Idempotency-Key with every write

`POST /v1/designs`, `POST /v1/prints`, `POST /v1/prints/{id}/orders` and
`POST /v1/orders` take an optional `Idempotency-Key` header. Pick a key that
names the thing you are making, once, and send the same key every time you
send that request: your order line id and the step, for instance. A
connected store sends its integration key (`ik_live_…`) where this shows the
secret key.

```http
POST /v1/prints/c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f/orders
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...
Idempotency-Key: WEB-10482-1:order
Content-Type: application/json
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/prints/{id}/orders request -->
```json
{
  "quantity": 1,
  "externalRef": "WEB-10482-1",
  "recipient": { "name": "Alexandra Lind", "email": "alexandra.lind@example.com" },
  "shippingAddress": {
    "line1": "12 High Street",
    "postalCode": "SW1A 1AA",
    "city": "London",
    "country": "GB"
  }
}
```

Without the header, each request is a new order, held to the rule below
that a design has one live order.

A key is 1 to 255 printable ASCII characters; anything else is refused `422 invalid_idempotency_key`. A key is remembered for 24 hours after it is first sent. While the first request is still being answered, a repeat is refused `409 idempotency_key_in_use` with a `Retry-After` of at most 2 seconds.

## What a repeat answers

What happens to a request sent again with the same key depends on what the
first one did:

| The first request | A repeat with the same key and body |
| --- | --- |
| succeeded | is answered with what the first made, marked `Idempotent-Replayed: true`, and makes nothing |
| is still being answered | `409 idempotency_key_in_use`; wait for `Retry-After` and send it again |
| was refused (a 4xx) | runs again: a refusal made nothing, so the key is free |
| failed for a reason of the API's own (a 5xx) | runs again, unless it had already made something, which it then answers |

A key sent with a different body, or to another route, is refused
`422 idempotency_key_reused`, and nothing is made: a key names one request.
Key order and spacing in the JSON do not count as a difference.

A repeat is answered with the thing the first request made, read as it is
now, not a stored copy of the first response:

- a commit answers `{ "designId": ... }`, the design the first request
  committed, even once that design has been deleted;
- a print answers as `GET /v1/prints/{id}` reads it now: `202` while it
  renders, its job ticket once it has, and `render_failed` once it failed;
- an order answers the order as `GET /v1/orders/{id}` reads it, with its
  current status. An address erased since stays erased.

An order a partner printshop refused is still a `201`, recorded as `failed`,
so a repeat answers that failed order rather than asking the printshop again.
To try a failed order again, use `POST /v1/orders/{id}/retry`.

Keys are shared by every secret key of your workspace, so a retry that
crosses a key rotation still finds the first request. A connected store's
keys belong to its site, so a retry sent after the store reconnected, under
its new integration key, still finds the first request too. A publishable key
and each studio member have keys of their own.


## Another caller's order of the same design

A key belongs to the caller that sent it, so it settles your own retry, not
another caller's order. When your store orders a design at checkout and the
workspace's automation, or someone in the studio, orders the same design, the
two requests carry different keys. That case is the API's: a design has one
live order, an order of it in any status but `failed` and `cancelled`. An
order of prints of a design that has one, or naming such a design, is refused
`409 design_already_ordered`, and nothing is written:

<!-- example: POST /v1/orders 409 -->
```json
{
  "error": "design_already_ordered",
  "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
  "orderId": "e1f2a3b4-c5d6-4e7f-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b"
}
```

`orderId` is the design's newest live order: read it with
`GET /v1/orders/{id}` rather than ordering again. Two orders of one design
sent at the same moment place one, and the other is refused naming it.

A repeat of your own request with its key is checked first, so a store
retrying after a timeout gets its order back with `Idempotent-Replayed: true`,
never this refusal. To order a design again on purpose, a second shirt for the
same customer, send `"reorder": true` in the body: the order is placed
whatever orders the design has. Retrying a failed order
(`POST /v1/orders/{id}/retry`, or `replacesOrderId`) needs no `reorder`, since
a failed order is not live.
## A proof token commits once

A proof token can be committed into one design only. Committing it again,
with another key or none, is refused, and the answer names the design the
token already became:

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs 409 -->
```json
{
  "error": "proof_already_committed",
  "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c"
}
```

Treat this as the commit having happened: carry on with that `designId`. It
is what a checkout that lost the first response, and retried without a key,
needs to recover.

## Approve and reject can be sent again

`POST /v1/designs/{id}/approve` and `POST /v1/designs/{id}/reject` take no
`Idempotency-Key`: the design's own status says whether the decision was
made. Send the decision again, with the same `expectedRevision`, when you did
not get its answer:

| The design is | Approving now again | Rejecting again |
| --- | --- | --- |
| approved at that revision | `200 { "status": "approved" }`, nothing recorded | `409 not_committed` |
| rejected at that revision | `409 not_committed` | `200 { "ok": true }`, nothing recorded |
| decided at another revision | `409 not_committed` | `409 not_committed` |

A repeat records no second audit entry and sends no second
`design.approved` or `design.rejected`. Without `expectedRevision`, a repeat
matches the design at whatever revision it was decided, so send the revision
you read when it matters which one was approved. A `409 not_committed`
means the design stands as some other decision left it: read it before
acting.

Each decision's event says what was decided: `design.approved` and
`design.rejected` carry the `revision` they decided, and `design.approved`
the `consent` kept with it, so a store can tell an approval of an older
revision from one of the design its customer last saw without reading the
design.

## Tie each record to your own

Every write in the path takes your own reference, `externalRef`, kept exactly
as you sent it, never required to be unique, and never read by Pixonaut:

- `POST /v1/designs` takes it from a secret or integration key (a publishable
  key sending it is refused `secret_key_required`).
  `GET /v1/designs?externalRef=` finds the designs holding it, and
  `PUT /v1/designs/{id}/external-ref` replaces it, for instance once a cart
  becomes an order:

<!-- example: PUT /v1/designs/{id}/external-ref request -->
```json
{ "externalRef": "WEB-10482-1" }
```

- `POST /v1/prints/{id}/orders` and `POST /v1/orders` take it for the order,
  and hand it to the printshop on the job ticket. `GET /v1/orders?externalRef=`
  finds the orders holding it.

When you are unsure whether a request that timed out went through, and the
key's window has passed, look the record up by your reference before sending
it again.

## Delete a design that was never bought

A design committed for a cart the customer then abandoned can be deleted
with `DELETE /v1/designs/{id}`, using the secret or integration key. It
disappears from every list and read, its share links stop working, and its
proof and pictures are released. It answers `204`, and `design.deleted` is
sent to your webhook endpoints:

<!-- example: webhook design.deleted -->
```json
{
  "id": "1790000000000-0192f5a4-7c1e-4d3a-9b6e-2f4c8a1d5e71",
  "type": "design.deleted",
  "createdAt": 1790000000000,
  "payload": { "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c" }
}
```

Only a design nothing was made of can go: one that was approved is refused
`409 design_approved`, and one that was printed `409 design_printed`, whether
or not it was corrected since. A design that was bought stays, with its
prints and orders; erase the personal data it holds instead
([Erasing personal data](#tag/erasing-personal-data)).
tags.name: Placing an order safely

tags.description:
A store connects to Pixonaut without its merchant copying a key. The store
sends the merchant to the studio's consent screen, a member approves, and
the store exchanges the code it is sent back with for everything it needs:
an integration key, a publishable key bound to its address, and a webhook
endpoint at the store. The exchange follows OAuth's authorization code flow
with PKCE.

## 1. Make a PKCE pair

Before sending the merchant anywhere, make a verifier and its S256 challenge
on your server, and keep the verifier with the merchant's session:

```js
import crypto from "node:crypto";

// 43 base64url characters, within RFC 7636's 43 to 128.
const VERIFIER_BYTES = 32;

// Keep `verifier` on your server; send `challenge` to /connect.
export function makePkcePair() {
  const verifier = crypto
    .randomBytes(VERIFIER_BYTES)
    .toString("base64url");
  const challenge = crypto
    .createHash("sha256")
    .update(verifier)
    .digest("base64url");
  return { verifier, challenge };
}
```

## 2. Send the merchant to the consent screen

Send the merchant's browser to the studio's `/connect` page with these query
parameters:

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `client` | The software the store runs: `woocommerce`. |
| `site_url` | The store's home address, such as `https://shop.acme.example`, with no query or fragment. |
| `redirect_uri` | Where the merchant is sent back: a page on the same origin as `site_url`. |
| `state` | A value of your own, returned untouched, to match the answer to the request. |
| `code_challenge` | The challenge from step 1. |
| `code_challenge_method` | `S256`, the only method taken. May be left out. |
| `site_name` | Optional: the store's own name, used in the integration key's name. |
| `environment` | Optional: `sandbox` to connect only to a workspace's sandbox, `live` to connect only to the live workspace. Left out, the member picks. |
| `rest_url` | Optional: the store's REST address, on the same origin as `site_url`, such as `https://shop.acme.example/?rest_route=/` for a WordPress site with plain permalinks. The webhook endpoint is registered under it. Left out, it is `<site_url>/wp-json/`. |

```http
GET /connect?client=woocommerce&site_url=https%3A%2F%2Fshop.acme.example&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fshop.acme.example%2Fwp-admin%2Fadmin.php%3Fpage%3Dpixonaut-connect&state=n_7f3a9c&code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM&code_challenge_method=S256&site_name=Acme%20Shop
```

A production deployment takes only `https` addresses for `site_url`,
`redirect_uri` and `rest_url`.

The merchant signs in if they need to, picks the workspace to connect, and
sees what the store will be able to do. Only a member who may manage API keys
(`api-keys:manage`) can approve. A workspace with a sandbox is offered as
**Live** or **Sandbox** (see Sandbox versus live, below), unless the request
names an `environment`.

On approval, the merchant is sent back to `redirect_uri` with `code` and your
`state` added to its query. If they cancel, they are sent back with
`error=access_denied` and your `state` instead.

## 3. Exchange the code

Check that `state` is the one you sent, then exchange the code from your
server, with the verifier and the same `redirect_uri`. The exchange takes no
API key: the code and the verifier are the proof.

A code can be exchanged once, within 60 seconds of the approval.

```http
POST /v1/connect/token
Content-Type: application/json
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/connect/token request -->
```json
{
  "code": "c_4f8a1d2e9b7c4a6f8e3d5b1a",
  "code_verifier": "dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk",
  "redirect_uri": "https://shop.acme.example/wp-admin/admin.php?page=pixonaut-connect"
}
```

The answer carries everything the store is given, each secret shown in this
response only. Store them all at once. `memberKey` links the member who
approved to the store: it is the key the store sends for the user who
connected it on Pixel's routes and the MCP endpoint (see Member key under
Authentication).

<!-- example: POST /v1/connect/token 201 -->
```json
{
  "tenantId": "0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000003",
  "tenantName": "Acme",
  "tenantSlug": "acme",
  "environment": "live",
  "reachable": true,
  "connectionId": "sc_0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000004",
  "integrationKey": {
    "id": "0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000005",
    "key": "ik_live_0123456789abcdef01234567",
    "label": "WooCommerce · Acme Shop (shop.acme.example)"
  },
  "publishableKey": {
    "id": "0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000006",
    "key": "pk_live_89abcdef0123456789abcdef",
    "allowedOrigins": ["https://shop.acme.example"]
  },
  "webhook": {
    "id": "0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000007",
    "url": "https://shop.acme.example/wp-json/pixonaut/v1/webhook",
    "secret": "whsec_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"
  },
  "memberKey": {
    "key": "mk_live_fedcba9876543210fedcba98",
    "memberId": "usr_0b1c2d3e4f504a6b8c7d0008",
    "memberName": "Alex Merchant",
    "memberEmail": "alex@acme.example"
  }
}
```

`environment` says which side of the workspace the store joined, `live` or
`sandbox`, and `tenantName` names the workspace; a sandbox is named after its
live workspace.

Any attempt uses the code up, and every refusal is the same
`400 invalid_grant`: an unknown or expired code, a `redirect_uri` that is not
the one approved, or a verifier that does not match the challenge. Whatever
went wrong, start again from step 1.

Connecting a site that is already connected replaces its connection: what it
was given before is revoked, and the new answer is all that works. A site is
matched by its address as written, so a store that moves from `http` to
`https`, or into another folder, connects as a new site.

## What the store is given

- **The integration key** (`ik_live_…`) is for the store's server. It acts
  for the workspace within what a store does: it reads templates, blanks and
  printshops, checks a print size, commits a customer's design (from the
  proof token its page drew, with the order details and its own reference),
  manages and deletes designs, makes and reads prints, places orders, manages
  its own webhook endpoint, and catches up on events with `GET /v1/events`.
  It never manages keys, members or settings. It is named after the store,
  and the audit record names the store's changes by that name.
- **The publishable key** (`pk_live_…`) is for the store's pages, where the
  designer runs. It is bound to the store's origin, and may take other
  hosts of the store's own domain too, such as its `www.` counterpart or a
  checkout on a host of its own (see Reading and changing the connection,
  below).
- **The webhook endpoint** is registered at the store, under its REST
  address, and receives the events the store may read, of the types it
  narrows them to, signed with `webhook.secret`
  ([Receive webhooks](#tag/receive-webhooks)).

The integration key reaches only what its own store made: the designs,
prints and orders made with a key its site was given (a design its pages
committed with the publishable key, or its hosted designer committed through
a link it handed out, included), and the share links it handed out. Another
store's design, print, order or link answers `404 not_found`, as one in
another workspace does, whether a path names it or a body does (a print of
its design, an order of its print), and the lists leave it out. Templates,
blanks and printshops are the workspace's, and every store reads them.

The webhook endpoint and `GET /v1/events` carry the same: events about the
store's own designs, prints and orders (every `order.*` event carries the
order's `externalRef`), and about templates, blanks and printshops. Events
about another store's work, or about inks, palettes, shapes, assets and
assistant runs, never reach it.

A store is its site. Reconnecting the same site, or connecting it again
after disconnecting, mints new keys, and the store keeps working with what
it made under the old ones; a request sent again with the same
`Idempotency-Key` is answered with what the first one made
([Placing an order safely](#tag/placing-an-order-safely)). A site that moves
to another address, http to https or into another folder included, is a new
store and starts with nothing.

What the store then does with them, from a customer's design to the order
arriving, is in
[A connected store, from connect to delivery](#tag/a-connected-store-from-connect-to-delivery).

## The store's webhook endpoint

To the integration key, the webhook routes reach its own endpoint alone:
`GET /v1/webhooks` lists that one, any other id is `404 not_found`, and it
cannot register another. It can read the endpoint's deliveries, ping it,
redeliver to it, switch it off and on, and choose the event types it
receives, with `PATCH /v1/webhooks/{id}`. Either field may be left out; an
empty `eventTypes` receives every type:

<!-- example: PATCH /v1/webhooks/{id} request -->
```json
{ "active": true, "eventTypes": ["design.committed", "order.status_changed"] }
```

The endpoint cannot be deleted on its own (`409 connection_endpoint`): it
goes with the store's other credentials when the store is disconnected.

### Where it is sent

The merchant's approval may name a `webhookUrl` for the endpoint, and
`PATCH /v1/webhooks/{id}` with a `url` changes it later. A store connected to a
sandbox may send it to any origin, such as a tunnel to a shop on a developer's
own machine; a live store must stay on its site's origin. Anything else is
`400 invalid_webhook_url`.

Pixonaut calls the address to check it, each time a `url` is sent, the address
it already has included. A live store is refused one that does not answer. A
sandbox store takes it and reads `reachable: false`, on the endpoint and in
`GET /v1/connect`: no delivery is enqueued, redelivering is
`409 endpoint_unreachable`, and the store reads its events with
`GET /v1/events`. Once the address moves or answers, events from then on are
delivered; what was waiting for the old one is dropped and is read by pulling,
so no backlog of attempts is queued.

The check at sending that refuses private addresses is the same for every
address, so a public tunnel works and a loopback address does not.

## Reading and changing the connection

The store reads its own connection with its integration key,
`GET /v1/connect`: its name as a member may have renamed it, its address,
the workspace and its environment, its webhook endpoint and the origins its
publishable key takes. Every other kind of key is `403 forbidden`.

The same read answers the workspace settings that change what the store's
customers and merchant get, as the studio's settings show them at that
moment, so a plugin can show them in its own settings screen or warn its
merchant:

- `branding`: what the hosted pages the store sends customers to are drawn
  in, the store's brand (see below): `brandId` names it, `logoUrl` loads its
  logo for a while (read the connection again for a fresh address), and
  `accentColor` is the `#rrggbb` the pages draw, an ink's screen colour when
  the accent follows one. The logo and the colour are null when none is set.
- `proofWatermark`: whether a newly rendered proof, the one a customer
  approves, carries a watermark.
- `deliverOrdersTo`: null when new orders ship to their customer, else the
  workspace's saved address they ship to instead, as `{ id, name }`.
- `printing`: `minPrintDpi`, `defaultBleedMm` and `defaultSafeAreaMm`, the
  defaults a template falls back to: the workspace's own, else the product's.
- `assetTtlHours`: how long a customer upload nothing holds is kept.
- `defaultLanguage`: the workspace's language, `en` until it chooses one,
  which its hosted pages and the designer are shown in when a link or a
  mount names no `locale`.

A store connected to a sandbox reads the sandbox's settings. None of them can
be changed with the integration key: a member changes them in the studio,
and `PATCH /v1/connect` refuses a body naming any of them as
`400 invalid_input`. The store's brand is the one exception.

<!-- example: GET /v1/connect 200 -->
```json
{
  "connectionId": "sc_0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000004",
  "name": "WooCommerce · Acme Shop (shop.acme.example)",
  "siteUrl": "https://shop.acme.example",
  "tenantId": "0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000003",
  "tenantName": "Acme",
  "tenantSlug": "acme",
  "environment": "live",
  "reachable": true,
  "webhookEndpointId": "wh_5f2a9c1d7e3b4a6f8c0d2e4a",
  "webhook": {
    "id": "wh_5f2a9c1d7e3b4a6f8c0d2e4a",
    "url": "https://shop.acme.example/wp-json/pixonaut/v1/webhook",
    "active": true,
    "reachable": true
  },
  "allowedOrigins": ["https://shop.acme.example"],
  "brandId": null,
  "printFileForm": null,
  "printFileTextTolerance": null,
  "branding": {
    "brandId": "br_3f6c1a2e-9b4d-4e7a-8c5f-000000000001",
    "logoUrl": "https://api.pixonaut.example/l/eyJhdWQiOiJsb2dvIn0.c2lnbmF0dXJl",
    "accentColor": "#1a73e8"
  },
  "brands": [
    {
      "id": "br_3f6c1a2e-9b4d-4e7a-8c5f-000000000001",
      "name": "Acme",
      "isDefault": true,
      "logoUrl": "https://api.pixonaut.example/l/eyJhdWQiOiJsb2dvIn0.c2lnbmF0dXJl",
      "accentColor": "#1a73e8"
    },
    {
      "id": "br_3f6c1a2e-9b4d-4e7a-8c5f-000000000002",
      "name": "Acme Pets",
      "isDefault": false,
      "logoUrl": null,
      "accentColor": "#2e7d32"
    }
  ],
  "proofWatermark": false,
  "deliverOrdersTo": null,
  "printing": {
    "minPrintDpi": 150,
    "defaultBleedMm": 3,
    "defaultSafeAreaMm": 3,
    "printFileForm": "flat",
    "printFileTextTolerance": { "value": 1, "unit": "px" }
  },
  "assetTtlHours": 168,
  "defaultLanguage": "en"
}
```

A store whose pages also run on other hosts of its own domain, its
counterpart with or without `www.`, a checkout or a headless storefront,
adds them to its publishable key without connecting again, with
`PATCH /v1/connect`:

<!-- example: PATCH /v1/connect request -->
```json
{
  "additionalOrigins": [
    "https://www.shop.acme.example",
    "https://checkout.acme.example"
  ]
}
```

The rule is the store's own domain, and nothing beyond it:

- **With the integration key**, any host on the site's registrable domain,
  as the [Public Suffix List](https://publicsuffix.org/) draws it, with the
  site's scheme and port. A store at `https://example.com` may add
  `https://www.example.com`, `https://checkout.example.com` or
  `https://shop.eu.example.com`. One at `https://shop.co.uk` may not add
  `https://other.co.uk`, and each site under a hosting suffix such as
  `github.io` is its own domain. A site at an IP address or at a host with no
  dot (`localhost`) may add nothing.
- **Anything else needs a member**, who mints a publishable key for it on the
  studio's **API Keys** page. An origin on another domain, a wildcard, an
  origin with a path, or another scheme or port is `400 invalid_origin`,
  naming the origin, and nothing changes.

Each origin is written as a browser's `Origin` header spells it,
`https://checkout.acme.example`, with no path or trailing slash. The key
takes up to 10 besides the site's own; more is `400 too_many_origins`, naming
the limit. An origin added this way admits the designer with the store's
publishable key, and a designer link's `returnUrl` may point to it. The
site's own origin is always kept and listed first, an empty list takes the
others away, and connecting again starts from the site's own origin.

## Choosing the store's brand

A workspace that sells under several names keeps a brand for each: a name, a
logo and an accent colour. Every hosted page a store's key hands out, the
proof pages it emails, correction links and designer links, is drawn in the
store's brand. A store with none of its own is drawn in the workspace's
default, and `GET /v1/connect` answers `brandId: null`.

`brands` lists the workspace's brands, the default first, each with its
`id`, `name`, `isDefault`, `logoUrl` and `accentColor`, so a plugin can offer
them in its own settings screen. The store chooses one with
`PATCH /v1/connect`, or goes back to the default with `null`:

<!-- example: PATCH /v1/connect request -->
```json
{ "brandId": "br_3f6c1a2e-9b4d-4e7a-8c5f-000000000002" }
```

An id that is not one of the workspace's brands is `404 brand_not_found`,
and nothing changes. A member may choose the store's brand in the studio too,
on the **API Keys** page, and every change is in the workspace's audit log.
A link keeps the brand it was created in: a change applies to the links
created after it. A brand a store is drawn in cannot be deleted, and
connecting the same site again keeps its brand.

## Listing and disconnecting

A store disconnects itself with its own integration key,
`DELETE /v1/connect`, which answers `204`. Call it when the merchant
disconnects the store from its own settings, or before the store is removed.

Members see every connected store, with its address and who approved it, on
the studio's **API Keys** page, and disconnect one there.

Disconnecting revokes all three credentials at once, and every share link the
store's key handed out. None of them can be revoked alone: a store with no
publishable key, or no endpoint, would be half connected.

## Sandbox versus live

A workspace with a sandbox is offered on the consent screen as **Live** or
**Sandbox**, Live unless the member picks otherwise. A store that knows which
it wants sends `environment=sandbox` (or `live`) with its request, and the
member is offered only that side. Connect a staging store
to the sandbox. Everything it is given then belongs to the sandbox, and its
keys say so: `ik_test_…` and `pk_test_…` where a live store's read `_live_`.
A test key works on the sandbox alone, and an order placed in a sandbox never
reaches a printshop. The exchange, the answer and every route are the same
for both.
tags.name: Connecting a store

tags.description:
A connected store holds two keys and no secret key: its **integration key**
(`ik_live_…`), for its server, and its **publishable key** (`pk_live_…`),
for its pages, where the designer runs. This guide follows one customer's
item through such a store, from the store connecting to the order arriving,
and names the key each call takes. Every call below that the store's server
makes takes its integration key, which reaches the store's own designs,
prints, orders and share links, and the workspace's templates, blanks and
printshops ([Connecting a store](#tag/connecting-a-store)).

| Step | Who calls | Key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The customer approves a proof | The store's page, or a hosted page | Publishable key, or the hosted page's link |
| Commit, re-reference, read, delete a design | The store's server | Integration key |
| Approve a design, hand out a proof page | The store's server | Integration key |
| Print and order | The store's server | Integration key |
| Hear what happened | Pixonaut, to the store's endpoint | Signed with the endpoint's secret |
| Catch up on missed events | The store's server | Integration key |

## 1. Connect

The merchant clicks connect in the store, approves in the studio, and the
store exchanges the code it is sent back with for its integration key, its
publishable key and its webhook endpoint
([Connecting a store](#tag/connecting-a-store)). Keep the integration key and
the endpoint's secret on the store's server, and hand only the publishable
key to its pages.

## 2. The customer approves a proof

On the product page, the designer runs with the publishable key, and the
customer approves what they made: `approve()` renders a proof and answers a
`proofToken` and a `proofUrl`. A store that sends its customer to the hosted
designer instead gets the `proofToken` back on its return address
([Sending the customer back to the store](#tag/sending-the-customer-back-to-the-store)).
Either way, nothing is stored yet: the token is the customer's approved
picture, waiting for the store to commit it.

The token reached the store through the customer's browser. Keep it with the
cart line on the store's server once the line is priced, and commit that copy
([Cart lifetimes and proof expiry](#tag/cart-lifetimes-and-proof-expiry)).

## 3. Commit the design with the store's reference

The store's server commits the proof with its integration key, with the cart
line as its own reference, `externalRef`, and any order data its printshop
needs:

```http
POST /v1/designs
Authorization: Bearer ik_live_...
Idempotency-Key: cart-10482-1:commit
Content-Type: application/json
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs request -->
```json
{
  "proofToken": "eyJhdWQiOiJwcm9vZiIsImlkIjoicHJmXzljMWUyZDNmNGE1YjZjN2Q4ZTlmMGExYiIsInQiOiJhY21lIiwiZXhwIjoxNzkyNDkxMjQ3MDAwfQ.EXAMPLE_signature_not_a_real_one_0000000000",
  "externalRef": "cart-10482-1",
  "fulfilmentPayload": { "variantSku": "TEE-BLACK-M" }
}
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs 201 -->
```json
{
  "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
  "printFloorDpi": 150,
  "lowResolution": []
}
```

`externalRef`, `fulfilmentPayload` and `printshopId` are a server's fields:
the store's page, with its publishable key, is refused them
`secret_key_required`. A proof token commits once; committing it again answers
`409 proof_already_committed` with the design it became
([Placing an order safely](#tag/placing-an-order-safely)).

Before taking payment, read the design back with `GET /v1/designs/{id}` and
check its print size, template and product against what the line was priced
as ([Cart lifetimes and proof expiry](#tag/cart-lifetimes-and-proof-expiry)).

When the cart becomes an order, point the design at the order line with
`PUT /v1/designs/{id}/external-ref`:

<!-- example: PUT /v1/designs/{id}/external-ref request -->
```json
{ "externalRef": "WEB-10482-1" }
```

`GET /v1/designs?externalRef=WEB-10482-1` then finds it.

## 4. Approve it, with the customer's consent

Once the customer has paid, the store's server approves the design with
`POST /v1/designs/{id}/approve`, and says how the customer agreed, so the
design keeps it: by adding it to the cart, by ticking a box, or by approving
it again on the store after correcting it (`edit`). `ref` is the store's own
reference for where it was given:

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs/{id}/approve request -->
```json
{
  "consent": { "kind": "checkbox", "at": 1790000050000, "ref": "WEB-10482" },
  "expectedRevision": 1
}
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs/{id}/approve 200 -->
```json
{ "status": "approved" }
```

`design.approved` carries the consent and the revision it approved:

<!-- example: webhook design.approved -->
```json
{
  "id": "1790000060000-5d7e1f2a-3b4c-4d5e-8f60-718293a4b5c6",
  "type": "design.approved",
  "createdAt": 1790000060000,
  "payload": {
    "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
    "approvedVia": "explicit",
    "revision": 1,
    "consent": { "kind": "checkbox", "at": 1790000050000, "ref": "WEB-10482" }
  }
}
```

`afterDays` approves later instead, and `expectedRevision` refuses the
approval `revision_changed` when the design was corrected since the store
read it ([Design to order](#tag/design-to-order)).

## 5. Or let the customer decide on a proof page

A store that wants the customer to approve the finished proof, rather than
approving it on their behalf, hands out a deciding proof page with
`POST /v1/share-links` and sends the customer its `url`, by email or from
their account page:

<!-- example: POST /v1/share-links request -->
```json
{
  "kind": "proof-page",
  "subjectId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
  "mayDecide": true,
  "locale": "sv"
}
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/share-links 201 -->
```json
{
  "id": "0b1c2d3e-4f50-4a6b-8c7d-000000000010",
  "kind": "proof-page",
  "subjectId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
  "mayDecide": true,
  "returnUrl": null,
  "name": null,
  "brandId": null,
  "designLimit": null,
  "printAreaFrame": false,
  "placementFrame": false,
  "locale": "sv",
  "createdAt": 1790000050000,
  "expiresAt": 1792592050000,
  "token": "EXAMPLE_share_link_token_not_a_real_one_000",
  "url": "https://app.pixonaut.example/h/proof/EXAMPLE_share_link_token_not_a_real_one_000?lang=sv"
}
```

The customer approves, rejects or asks for changes there. An approval on the
page keeps a `proof_page` consent naming the link, and emits
`design.approved` as above; a request for changes emits
`design.changes_requested`, and with a `returnUrl` the page sends the
customer back to the store to correct the design
([Sending the customer back to the store](#tag/sending-the-customer-back-to-the-store)).
A link the store's key handed out stops working when the store disconnects.

## 6. Print and order

`POST /v1/prints` makes the approved design's print files, answering `202`
while it renders; once `GET /v1/prints/{id}` reads `completed`, or
`print.completed` arrives, `POST /v1/prints/{id}/orders` sends the completed
print to the printshop,
with the order line as `externalRef` and who it ships to:

```http
POST /v1/prints/c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f/orders
Authorization: Bearer ik_live_...
Idempotency-Key: WEB-10482-1:order
Content-Type: application/json
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/prints/{id}/orders request -->
```json
{
  "quantity": 1,
  "externalRef": "WEB-10482-1",
  "recipient": { "name": "Alexandra Lind", "email": "alexandra.lind@example.com" },
  "shippingAddress": {
    "line1": "12 High Street",
    "postalCode": "SW1A 1AA",
    "city": "London",
    "country": "GB"
  }
}
```

An item printed on several placements is ordered as one with
`POST /v1/orders` ([Front and back on one item](#tag/front-and-back-on-one-item)).
Send an `Idempotency-Key` with each, so a retried request makes nothing twice
([Placing an order safely](#tag/placing-an-order-safely)). What each answers,
and what the order goes through from there, is in
[Design to order](#tag/design-to-order). The integration key also cancels an
order (`POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel`), retries a failed one
(`POST /v1/orders/{id}/retry`), and settles one whose outcome is unknown
(`PATCH /v1/orders/{id}`).

## 7. Hear what happened, and catch up

The store's endpoint receives the events about the store's own work, and
about the workspace's templates, blanks and printshops, signed with the
endpoint's secret ([Receive webhooks](#tag/receive-webhooks)): the
design's `design.committed` and `design.approved`, the print's
`print.completed`, and the order's `order.submitted` and each
`order.status_changed` up to `shipped`. Narrow them to what the store handles
with `PATCH /v1/webhooks/{id}` on its own endpoint
([Connecting a store](#tag/connecting-a-store)).

A store that was down misses nothing for good. Deliveries are retried
([Webhooks](#tag/webhooks) gives the schedule), and the store's server pulls
the events in the order they were recorded with `GET /v1/events`, narrowed
with `types` to the ones it subscribes to. Keep the pull's own checkpoint,
the `id` of the last event a pull answered, and pass it as `after`; leave
`after` out on the first pull. Never move the checkpoint on because a webhook
arrived: deliveries can arrive out of order, and an event that failed while a
later one was delivered would then be skipped.

```http
GET /v1/events?after=1790000060000-5d7e1f2a-3b4c-4d5e-8f60-718293a4b5c6&types=order.status_changed
Authorization: Bearer ik_live_...
```

<!-- example: GET /v1/events 200 -->
```json
{
  "events": [
    {
      "id": "1790086400000-0f1e2d3c-4b5a-4968-8776-655443322110",
      "type": "order.status_changed",
      "createdAt": 1790086400000,
      "payload": {
        "orderId": "e1f2a3b4-c5d6-4e7f-8a9b-0c1d2e3f4a5b",
        "printId": "c4d5e6f7-a8b9-4c0d-9e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f",
        "status": "shipped",
        "previousStatus": "printed"
      }
    }
  ],
  "nextCursor": null
}
```

Each event comes in the envelope a delivery carries, with the same `id`, so
the store drops one it already handled by webhook. Follow `nextCursor` as the next
`after` until it is `null`. The pull answers the events the endpoint
receives: never one about another store's work.

## 8. Clean up a cart nobody bought

A design committed for a cart the customer abandons is deleted with
`DELETE /v1/designs/{id}`, which answers `204` and emits `design.deleted`.
A design that was approved or printed stays
([Placing an order safely](#tag/placing-an-order-safely)).

## 9. Erase a customer's personal data

When a customer asks to be erased, the store's server erases the delivery a
design holds with `DELETE /v1/designs/{id}/delivery`, and the recipient and
address of each order once it has shipped, failed or been cancelled, with
`POST /v1/orders/{id}/erase-personal-data`. It finds the orders by its own
reference, `GET /v1/orders?externalRef=`
([Erasing personal data](#tag/erasing-personal-data)).

## When the store goes away

Before the store is removed, or when the merchant disconnects it, the
store's server calls `DELETE /v1/connect` with its integration key. Its
integration key, its publishable key, its webhook endpoint and every share
link it handed out stop working at once. Its designs, prints and orders
stay with the workspace, and the same site connecting again keeps working
with them ([Connecting a store](#tag/connecting-a-store)).
tags.name: A connected store, from connect to delivery

tags.description:
A store can send its customer to a page Pixonaut hosts and get them back to
its own: to make a design on the hosted designer, to correct one they already
made, or to decide a proof. The store's server hands out the page's link,
with its secret key or a connected store's integration key, naming where the
customer returns to and a `state` of its own. The page sends the customer
back with that `state`, and with the proof they approved when there is one.

| Page | Handed out with | Sends the customer back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hosted designer | `POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links` | On approving, with `state` and `proofToken`; on cancelling, with `state` |
| Hosted correction page | `POST /v1/designs/{id}/correction-links` | On approving, with `state` and `proofToken`; on cancelling, with `state` |
| Proof page | `POST /v1/share-links` | Once the customer asks for changes, with `state` |

## The return address

`returnUrl` is where the page sends the customer, and `state` is carried
back to it untouched: Pixonaut never reads it. Put in `state` whatever lets
the store match the customer to its own session, a cart key or a signed
nonce, and check it when the customer arrives. `state` is taken only with a
`returnUrl`.

`returnUrl` must be on one of the origins the workspace's publishable keys
are allowed on, so a connected store returns to its own site, and in
production it must be `https`. Otherwise the link is refused
`400 return_url_off_store` or `400 return_url_not_https`. It is fixed when the
link is handed out, so the page can be made to send the customer nowhere
else.

The page adds its parameters to the store's own query and keeps the rest of
the address as it was: `state`, and `proofToken` when it brings back a proof.
A `proofToken` already in `returnUrl` is dropped, and so is a `state` when
the link carries none; the link's own `state` replaces one already there.

## The hosted designer

A store that does not run the designer on its own page hands out a hosted
designer for one of its templates, with what it sells the template on: the
blank and placement, its size menu and its photos, as the SDK takes them on a
store's page.

```http
POST /v1/templates/tshirt-basic/designer-links
Authorization: Bearer ik_live_...
Content-Type: application/json
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links request -->
```json
{
  "blankId": "blank_tshirt",
  "placementId": "front",
  "printSizes": [
    { "widthMm": 280, "heightMm": 360, "label": "Large" },
    { "widthMm": 200, "heightMm": 257, "label": "Medium" }
  ],
  "returnUrl": "https://shop.acme.example/cart?add=tshirt-basic",
  "state": "cart-10482",
  "locale": "sv"
}
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links 201 -->
```json
{
  "id": "shl_9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f",
  "token": "EXAMPLE_designer_link_token_not_a_real_one",
  "url": "https://app.pixonaut.example/h/design/EXAMPLE_designer_link_token_not_a_real_one?lang=sv",
  "expiresAt": 1790086400000,
  "name": null,
  "brandId": null,
  "designLimit": null,
  "printAreaFrame": false,
  "placementFrame": false,
  "locale": "sv"
}
```

Send the customer to `url`. The link follows the template's live version.
A link carrying `state` names one shopper's visit and works for 24 hours after it is handed out; one without `state` works until it is withdrawn.

When the customer approves their design, the page makes a proof and sends
them to
`https://shop.acme.example/cart?add=tshirt-basic&state=cart-10482&proofToken=…`.
Nothing is stored yet: the store's server checks `state`, keeps the
`proofToken` with the cart line, and commits it with its key as a proof from
its own page is committed
([A connected store, from connect to delivery](#tag/a-connected-store-from-connect-to-delivery)).
If the customer cancels, they are sent to the same address with `state`
alone.

### One link for every customer

A store may hand out one designer link and send all its customers to it,
rather than one link per customer. Its stored `state` is then the same for
everyone, so the store names each customer's trip in the address instead:
take the link's `url` as it was handed out and add one query parameter,
`state=<value>`, before sending the customer there.

```
https://app.pixonaut.example/h/design/EXAMPLE_designer_link_token_not_a_real_one?lang=sv&state=trip-7f3a9c
```

The page returns that value as `state`, on approving and on cancelling, in
place of the link's own; the rest of the return address is as above. It
holds for the whole visit: a reload or a change of `lang` keeps it. The value
is 1 to 200 characters of `A–Z a–z 0–9 . _ ~ -`. An address with no `state`,
or one outside that form, returns the link's own `state`, or none when the
link has none; a value outside the form is never sent back. Pixonaut neither
checks nor keeps the value: matching it to the customer's trip is the
store's job, as with the link's own `state`.

A front and a back are one link with `sides`, which returns a proof for each
side under its key, `proofToken[front]=…&proofToken[back]=…`
([Front and back on one item](#tag/front-and-back-on-one-item)). Without a
`returnUrl`, the page commits the design itself and shows the customer its
id, and nothing is sent back to the store.

## Correcting a design from the store

A customer who wants to change a design they already made, from the cart or
after asking for changes, corrects that design rather than making a new one.
The store's server hands out a **correction link** for it:

```http
POST /v1/designs/6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c/correction-links
Authorization: Bearer ik_live_...
Content-Type: application/json
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs/{id}/correction-links request -->
```json
{
  "returnUrl": "https://shop.acme.example/account/designs?edit=6f1c8a2b",
  "state": "edit-7c1e"
}
```

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs/{id}/correction-links 201 -->
```json
{
  "id": "shl_5d0c9e3b7a1f2e4d6c8b0a91",
  "token": "EXAMPLE_correction_link_token_not_a_real_one",
  "url": "https://app.pixonaut.example/h/correct/EXAMPLE_correction_link_token_not_a_real_one",
  "expiresAt": 1790007200000,
  "name": null,
  "brandId": null
}
```

A correction link works for 2 hours after it is handed out, for that one design only.
A design that takes no correction, because it was rejected or one of its
prints has an order, is refused `409 not_editable`; duplicate an ordered one
instead ([Design to order](#tag/design-to-order)).

The link opens the design in one of two places:

- **On the store's own page.** Hand out the link with no `returnUrl`, and
  mount the designer with its `token`, from an origin the store's
  publishable key allows:

  ```js
  const designer = await Pixonaut.mount('#pixonaut', {
    correctionLink: token,
    design: designId,
  });
  const { proofToken } = await designer.approve();
  ```

  `url` is then `null`: the link opens no page of its own.
- **On the hosted correction page.** With a `returnUrl`, send the customer to
  `url`. When they approve, the page sends them to
  `https://shop.acme.example/account/designs?edit=6f1c8a2b&state=edit-7c1e&proofToken=…`;
  when they cancel, to the same address with `state` alone.

Either way, approving makes a proof of the correction and changes nothing.
The store's server makes it the design's next revision with
`PATCH /v1/designs/{id}`, sending the proof's token with its key:

<!-- example: PATCH /v1/designs/{id} request -->
```json
{ "proofToken": "EXAMPLE_correction_proof_token_not_a_real_one" }
```

<!-- example: PATCH /v1/designs/{id} 200 -->
```json
{
  "revision": 2,
  "edited": true,
  "proofId": "prf_9c1e2d3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a1b",
  "printFloorDpi": 150,
  "lowResolution": []
}
```

With `edited: true`, the store receives `design.edited` with the new
revision. The design is back to `committed`, its approval cleared, so the
store approves it again once the customer has agreed, with an `edit` consent
and the new revision as `expectedRevision`:

<!-- example: POST /v1/designs/{id}/approve request -->
```json
{
  "consent": { "kind": "edit", "at": 1790000200000, "ref": "edit-7c1e" },
  "expectedRevision": 2
}
```

A customer who approves without changing anything leaves the design as it
was: the answer is `edited: false` with the current `revision` and proof, no
`design.edited` is sent, and an approval the design had stands. Branch on
`edited` rather than waiting for the event.

A design corrected elsewhere since the customer opened it refuses the
correction `409 revision_changed`: open it again, and the customer starts
from the design as it is now.

## The proof page

A deciding proof page, handed out as the store's server hands out any proof
page ([A connected store, from connect to delivery](#tag/a-connected-store-from-connect-to-delivery)),
can send the customer back to the store once they have asked for changes, so
the store opens the design for them to correct. Name the return address, the
`state`, and the language the page is shown in:

<!-- example: POST /v1/share-links request -->
```json
{
  "kind": "proof-page",
  "subjectId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
  "mayDecide": true,
  "returnUrl": "https://shop.acme.example/account/designs?edit=6f1c8a2b",
  "state": "edit-7c1e",
  "locale": "sv"
}
```

Once the customer's request is taken, the page sends them to
`https://shop.acme.example/account/designs?edit=6f1c8a2b&state=edit-7c1e`,
with nothing else; `design.changes_requested` carries what they asked. The
store then hands out a correction link, as above. Approving and rejecting
keep the customer on the page. A link with a return keeps a proof page's own
lifetime: a customer may sit on a proof for weeks. Without `returnUrl`, the
page keeps the customer and says their request was sent. `locale` is any
customer-facing language, by its code, and the link's `url` then carries
`?lang=<locale>`; absent, the page is in the workspace's default language.
tags.name: Sending the customer back to the store

tags.description:
A share link is known by what it opens, and two designer links for one
template read alike. A link can carry a **name** of the workspace's own, a
designer link's address is **kept** so it can be copied again, any other
link's lost address can be **regenerated**, and a designer link can **limit**
how many designs its page makes.

## A link's name

`name` is taken by every route that hands a link out
(`POST /v1/share-links`, `POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links`,
`POST /v1/designs/{id}/correction-links`) and changed with
`PATCH /v1/share-links/{id}`, where `null` removes it. The page the link
opens never shows it.

A name is at most 80 characters once trimmed, with its inner spaces made one.
It names one working link of the workspace, case aside, so an automation can
find a link by it: a second link given a name another working link holds is
refused `409 share_link_name_taken`, naming the holder. A withdrawn or expired
link frees its name.

Check a name as it is typed, before handing a link out:

```http
GET /v1/share-links?name=Spring%20market%20stand&pageSize=1
```

An automation keeps the id of the link it was pointed at, not its name, so a
rename never breaks it. A design made through a link names it:
`design.committed` carries `shareLinkId`, and the design reads it as
`shareLinkId`.

<!-- example: PATCH /v1/share-links/{id} request -->
```json
{ "name": "Spring market stand" }
```

## A designer link's address

A designer link sits on a store's product page until withdrawn, so its
address is kept: `GET /v1/share-links` answers it as `url` to whoever may
manage the link. Every other kind is private to one customer, order or
printshop, and its address is shown once, in the response that handed it out;
its `url` on the list is null. So is a designer link's handed out before
addresses were kept, until it is regenerated.

## A new address for the same link

`POST /v1/share-links/{id}/regenerate` gives a working link a new address and
answers it once. The old address opens nothing from then on; the link keeps
its id, settings, expiry, history and design count. A designer link whose
address is kept is refused `409 address_kept`: copy it again instead.

## A designer link's design limit

`designLimit` limits the designs a designer link's page makes: `count`, from
1 to 10,000, in a `period` of `total`, or a rolling `hour`, `day` or `week`
(the last 60 minutes, 24 hours or 7 days). Set it when handing the link out
or with `PATCH /v1/share-links/{id}`; `null` removes it.

Each side the page approves counts one: a front and a back count two. Without
a return address the page commits each design, which counts. With one, the
page hands the store a proof, which counts; the store's commit of that proof
carries the link and is not counted again. Previews, abandoned visits and the
store's own commits from elsewhere do not count.

At the limit, the page shows the customer when the link opens again, or, for
a limit in total, to ask the shop for a new link. An approval that would pass
the limit is refused whole, with when the link opens again: the moment the
oldest design counted leaves the window, or null for a limit in total.

<!-- example: POST /v1/templates/{id}/designer-links request -->
```json
{
  "name": "Market stall, 50 a day",
  "designLimit": { "count": 50, "period": "day" }
}
```
tags.name: Naming, keeping and limiting share links

tags.description:
An **event** is a fact about the tenant's product state that an integration
may want to react to: a design committed, a print completed, an order's status
changing. Each event is sent as a signed `POST` to every webhook endpoint
subscribed to its type. The body is the same envelope for every type, with the
payload described under each event below:

<!-- example: webhook design.committed -->
```json
{
  "id": "1790000000000-0192f5a4-7c1e-4d3a-9b6e-2f4c8a1d5e70",
  "type": "design.committed",
  "createdAt": 1790000000000,
  "payload": {
    "designId": "6f1c8a2b-3d4e-4f5a-8b6c-7d8e9f0a1b2c",
    "templateId": "tshirt-basic@2",
    "apiKeyId": "3b2d9c1e-5a4f-4e7d-8c6b-1a0f9e8d7c6b"
  }
}
```

A webhook endpoint is registered in the studio, or by your server with its
secret key (`POST /v1/webhooks`), each optionally narrowed to a set of event
types. Each endpoint has its own signing secret, shown once when it is
registered. A secret key lists and manages only the endpoints it registered
itself, and they are deleted with it; the studio shows and manages every
endpoint.

## Verifying a request

Every request is signed with the endpoint's secret. Verify it before trusting
the body:

| Header | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `x-pixonaut-timestamp` | When this attempt was sent, in Unix seconds. |
| `x-pixonaut-signature` | `v1=` followed by the hex HMAC-SHA256, keyed with the endpoint's signing secret, of the `x-pixonaut-timestamp` value, a `.`, and the raw request body. |

Refuse a request whose `x-pixonaut-timestamp` is more than 300 seconds from your own clock. A later signature scheme would be sent in the same header beside `v1=`, comma-separated, so check the `v1=` value and ignore any other.

Compare the signature in constant time, over the raw body bytes as they
arrived, before parsing them: re-serialising parsed JSON changes the bytes.
The timestamp is the moment that attempt was sent, not when the event
happened, so a retry of an old event still verifies, and a copy of an earlier
attempt replayed later does not.

To test a verifier, `webhook-signature-vectors.json`, published with every API
release beside this reference (`/api/<version>/` on the CDN), holds requests signed by the same code that
signs every delivery: ones a correct verifier accepts, and ones it refuses,
among them a request sent longer ago than the tolerance and a signature
header without its scheme. Run your verifier with its clock at the file's
`now` (Unix seconds).

## Acknowledging, retries and redelivery

Answer any `2xx` to acknowledge a request. Anything else, a redirect, or no
answer in time is a failed attempt. A **delivery** (one event sent to one
endpoint) is retried until the endpoint accepts it or the retries run out, at
which point it has failed and stays failed until someone redelivers it.

A delivery is tried at most 22 times. The gap before each retry grows, from 30 seconds after the first failed attempt to 3.7 hours before the last, so the retries run out about 27.6 hours after the first attempt.

To **redeliver** is to send a delivery again from the start, with a fresh set
of retries: a failed one, or a delivered one the receiver lost. It is done
from the endpoint's delivery log in the studio, or by the secret key that
registered it (a connected store's endpoint, by the store's integration key):
one delivery (`POST /v1/webhooks/{id}/deliveries/{deliveryId}/redeliver`), or
every failed one at once after downtime
(`POST /v1/webhooks/{id}/deliveries/redeliver-failed`). Either can also send a
test request (a ping) on demand. A ping is not an event: it is signed the same
way but never retried, and its `type` is not one an endpoint can subscribe to.

A retry or a redelivery carries the same event `id`, so drop a request whose
`id` you have already handled. Deliveries can arrive out of order; use
`createdAt` to order events about the same thing.

## Missed deliveries

Your server can also pull the events it may have missed, in the order they
were recorded, with `GET /v1/events?after=<event id>`: give it the `id` of
the last event a previous pull answered, leaving `after` out the first time,
and narrow it with `types` (comma-separated) to the types your endpoint
subscribes to. Keep that checkpoint apart from the deliveries you receive:
deliveries can arrive out of order, so the last one handled can be later
than one still being retried. Each event comes in the same envelope
a delivery's body carries. Follow `nextCursor` as the next `after` until it is
`null`, when you have caught up.

## Rules a receiver can rely on

- An endpoint registered with an empty set of event types receives every type. New types are added over time, and a subscription to every type receives them as they appear, so a receiver ignores types it does not know.
- An update event names the fields the change set, without claiming their values differ from before.

post.description: A template was paused or resumed: `live: false` is a pause, after which customers cannot design on it, and `live: true` a resume. Sent once per template that flipped, whether one template or several were switched, and never for a switch to the state it already had. A store that missed a delivery, or connected after the switch, reads `status` on `GET /v1/templates/{id}`, which is the state to trust.

automation.description: The automation that caused the event, beside `via`.

id.description: The automation's id.

name.description: What the automation was called when it acted.

createdAt.description: When the event happened, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

id.description: The event's id. A retry or a redelivery carries the same id, so a receiver can drop one it has already handled.

endpointId.description: The webhook endpoint the ping tests.

via.description: `automation` when one of your automations caused the event; absent otherwise.

db_error.description: The api could not read or write its database.

feature_disabled.description: The tenant does not have the feature the key is for: `api` for a publishable or secret key, `mcp` for an MCP key. The key is kept, and is admitted again once the tenant has the feature.

forbidden.description: The route does not take the kind of credential sent.

member_link_required.description: A connected store's integration key was sent to a route that acts as a member. The store links its user's Pixonaut account first (`POST /v1/connect/token` with `kind: "member_link"`) and sends the member key it is given.

member_link_revoked.description: A member key whose link no longer holds: it was revoked, its member left the workspace, or its store was disconnected. The store asks its user to link their account again. The store's own connection is not affected.

origin_forbidden.description: A publishable key was sent from an origin outside the key's allowlist.

payload_too_large.description: The request body is larger than the route accepts. `maxBytes` is the limit.

rate_limited.description: Too many requests in the current window. Retry after the number of seconds in `retry-after`.

secret_key_required.description: The route takes a secret key, and the request carried another credential.

unauthorized.description: The request carries no credential, or one that is unknown or revoked.

workspace_suspended.description: The workspace the credential belongs to is suspended. Every credential of it is refused until the suspension is lifted; nothing of it is deleted.
